text: Switching to new equipment and technology requires heavy capital investments upfront by the waste collection companies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Although companies would save manpower costs in the long run, the upfront cost of buying a new fleet of side loading vehicles is a significant investment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They will also need to consider their contract duration with NEA.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is a big business risk for the waste companies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, to drive change and adoption, Government grants and longer contract periods must be provided to allow these companies to sustain.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If the Government is able to assist them, these companies must move towards the right direction, to leverage better design, more efficient work processes and use technology to address challenges.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They must continue to think creatively and work fast to implement innovative solutions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Currently, with higher wages and heavier investments, waste management companies will be faced with higher operating overheads.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Consumers will also be expected to assist in the cost increase.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Cost increase will always be a contentious concern especially with the rising costs of living.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, a fairer approach towards cost increase is inevitable and the waste collection fees will have to be better structured based on a fair user-pays costing principle.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is a flat fee structure and does not take into consideration the number of occupants and the amount of waste that is generated within each household.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The current flat fee structure is easy to administer but it does not incentivise occupants to reduce their waste generated.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We could consider implementing a more sophisticated data management software, to vary waste collection fees according to the size of each household.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This way, a higher fee could be applied appropriately.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If everyone consumes less, recycles more and generates less waste, we will all be able to fundamentally cope with our national waste management and reduce the waste generated.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Social responsibility and civic-mindedness are key to any good solution.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At home and at the workplace, we should sort and pack waste according to wet or dry waste, so that they do not mess up the trash bins or create foul odours and attract pests.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These considerations will help to keep our trash bins cleaner and less smelly, making the collection job easier for the crew.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Compared to most countries, dumping waste in Singapore is a relatively fuss-free activity because of the ubiquitous presence of trash bins.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Truth be told, we may have become victims of our own success because these bins would require a lot of workers to clear on a regular basis, whether they are full or not.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To reduce the manpower required, we should rethink how we can effectively reduce waste collection requirements.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For instance, for certain areas, NParks and Town Councils could consider using bigger bins, reducing the number of trash bins and place them further apart in public places.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This will reduce the number of collection trips and the staff that is needed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: But that also means people must be prepared to walk further to dispose of their trash and going to another trash bin if the nearest one is already full.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should recycle more and be more environmentally friendly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, we have stepped up our recycling culture and have seen encouraging improvements.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, our recycling rate is still lagging behind countries such as Germany and South Korea.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should continue with more public education efforts and recycling drives to encourage ground-up recycling practices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As mentioned, it will take strong civic-mindedness and social responsibility to encourage people to be more conscious about recycling and proper disposal of their litter.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Such lifelong habits are best learnt in schools and at home from a young age.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should all try to be more considerate and care about the welfare of our fellow Singaporeans who are working hard to assist us to clear our waste on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Let us do our part and not make their job harder than it already is.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am thus very heartened to read the further introduction of the Environmental Public Health (Amendment) Bill, with a focus on issues close to the hearts and lives of most of our residents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ensuring a cleaner living environment in our estates and uplifting the waste management and cleaning sector in Singapore are areas I believe to be important to attain high public health standards for a better quality of life for all Singaporeans, including my residents in Jalan Kayu.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A major concern I often hear from my residents is the high-rise littering of cigarette ashes and butts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many residents are not only asking for their homes to be kept clean and safe from such unwanted litters, but they also raised a valid fire safety concern, especially when the clothes that they hang out for drying catch the cigarette ashes and butts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our Town Council cleaners are often called upon to clean up these litters thrown down by irresponsible home owners or tenants, spreading the cleaners thin on their daily cleaning duties in the estate.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A stronger deterrent through adding clause 17A is a policy enhancement that I support to change behaviours and habits.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I hope to recommend that stronger penalties be imposed on high-rise littering re-offenders.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, a Corrective Work Order (CWO) for up to 12 hours can also be imposed by the Court.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For first-time offenders, a fine of $2,000 may be able to deter them from committing the offence further.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, for repeat offenders, I wonder if there are deeper habitual behavioural issues causing them not to be able to restrain themselves from such irresponsible actions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides monetary fines to seek behavioural changes, I suggest that a CWO be complemented with a mandatory education or counselling session for re-offenders so that we can address root causes leading to these re-offences.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although I understand the intention for these higher standards is to drive up public health standards of cleaning businesses, I would like to seek clarifications from MSE whether considerations have been given to potential cost increases that cleaning companies may face to meet these higher licensing requirements.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Cleaning companies are already facing manpower crunch and higher costs to implement the PWM.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Has MSE considered what further costs may cleaning companies need to incur to meet the requirements and who these costs will be passed to?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead of merely imposing higher licensing requirements, like my fellow hon Parliamentary Member, Ms Poh Li San, I would like to suggest for MSE to work across relevant agencies and Ministries to provide concurrently an automation and capabilities enhancement grant with platforms that cleaning companies can learn what practical and scalable automation they can utilise in their cleaning processes, such as enabling them with knowledge and grants or partnership with Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to experiment with technologies like cleaning robots in HDB flats to see how this technology needs to be iterated and enhanced for it to work in the estates at higher scalability.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope this will enable the cleaning companies to increase productivity even as they need to invest in more essential costs to keep higher standards.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very supportive of this move by MSE to legislate and enable workers from the waste management sector to benefit also from the PWM.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides baseline wage growth through PWM, I hope that the Government can consider the intangible aspects of the cleaning and waste management sectors by enhancing respect, dignity and appreciation for our cleaners and workers in these sectors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope MSE can strengthen tripartite cooperation within the sector to create platforms through the Government, employers and union to give social support and recognition to these workers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similar to the Migrant Workers' Centre Recreation Club, I would like to suggest that the Government work with the union to set up a recreation club for our cleaners and workers from the waste management sectors to better support their social recreational needs, mental well-being and to show appreciation for the hard work and dedication that these unsung heroes give to keep our environment clean.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I support the Environmental Public Health (Amendment) Bill tabled by NEA.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the Bill will add a new presumption clause to HDB high-rise littering cases to assume that the registered owner is the offender.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel that the addition will enhance the deterrent effect and the awareness of flat owners and tenants on public health issues and make them take on greater responsibility to prevent littering from their units.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that the Government will step up the education and disciplinary measures for repeat offenders and raise their awareness of environmental public health through compulsory education or Corrective Work Orders (CWO) programmes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I am also worried that requiring businesses to comply with the salaries set by the authorities will cause them to raise prices.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I hope that the Government will set up the waste management innovation fund to encourage businesses to adopt innovative and fully automated technology tools, as well as strengthen the staff training to raise productivity.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While raising the basic salary of workers, I also hope that the Government and unions will pay more attention to the welfare of waste management workers and cleaners.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I suggest providing better public social assistance and considering setting up a waste management worker recreation centre, similar to the Migrant Workers' Centre Recreation Club, to provide them with recreational activities to help them relax.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, let me end my speech with a quote by renowned conservationist, Dr Jane Goodall.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She said, "Each one of us matters, has a role to play, and makes a difference.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each one of us must take responsibility for our own lives, and above all, show respect and love for living things around us, especially each other." This quote comes close to my heart as I speak on this Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe everyone is responsible for keeping our community clean and liveable.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is the ultimate mark of mutual respect for one another to help take care of our environment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And let us all also do our part.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my speech today, I will focus on two.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is an essential step for our essential workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It includes paying workers a baseline wage, overtime and an annual bonus per the Tripartite Cluster for Waste Management's recommended wage schedule.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I understand that the wage schedule is expected to stretch to 30 June 2029.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I hope that this schedule can be shortened by increasing the opportunities to upskill workers and introduce technology.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Just last week, a resident approached me and shared his long-time frustration at a neighbour throwing a cigarette butt out of the window and onto his air-condition ledge and sometimes, into his room.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: He shared the difficulty the agencies had in catching the culprit despite the deployment of cameras and enhanced surveillance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Sometimes, litter in the form of food, face masks, tissue papers land in their rooms and it is certainly distressing especially if they have children or elderly family members at home.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Complaints about this similar issue have nearly doubled over the past few years, and it is imperative that we take swift and effective action to address it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite the increased deployment of cameras, the success in curbing high-rise littering has been incremental.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, I conducted house visits together with the Public Hygiene Council.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We sought residents' views on the proposed presumption law and were glad that every resident was supportive of this move.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Nevertheless, I understand that there may be some concerns regarding the implementation of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill's proposal of the presumption of guilt for flat owners and tenants may raise questions about due process and fairness.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could the Ministry share and elaborate further on its plans to ensure that members of the public understand the processes and their cases would be dealt with fairly?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, could the Ministry provide assurances and examples on how the enforcement process would consider the well-being of the elderly, young children and vulnerable groups, including those who are facing mental health issues?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Often, they are considered serial offenders and despite continuous intervention and support from their own family members, the Residents’ Committee (RC), the Town Council, NEA as well as the Police, they continue to litter.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Would the Ministry then consider working closely with the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), for example, to provide mandatory counselling support?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Similarly, this may be extended to the elderly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They would need to provide evidence within 14 days of being notified by NEA that an offence has been committed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This could be difficult especially if they were not present in the flat at the time of the offence or if the elderly, mentally or physically disabled are the ones who are involved.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While I have raised some concerns and suggestions, I am confident that the Ministry will address these issues fairly to all parties concerned.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is fundamental that Singaporeans play an active role to maintain high environmental and public health standards.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We cannot take things for granted and we must stand for a cleaner, greener Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In particular, I support clause 5, the new section 17A where the registered flat owner or registered flat tenant will be found guilty of high-rise littering if he cannot prove within a given time that he is not responsible for the offence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This reflects what I see and feel on the ground, as the complaints I received about high-rise littering increased significantly at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when most people were working from home.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Taking a step back from the proposed amendments, the success of whether we can even track the origin of high-rise litter stems from the effective installation of the surveillance cameras.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Minister Grace Fu has pointed out in the Parliament Sitting last October that cameras monitoring high-rise littering often failed to capture it in action.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Even if the high-rise littering could be recorded, NEA still has to take about three to six months to decide whether to issue a fine.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Such a process appears to be time-consuming and laborious.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, I also hope that NEA has deployed artificial intelligence (AI) to detect high-rise litter, rather than using human eyes to watch videos for hours to see if there is any litter falling from height.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is less effective if you use human eyes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Even if we finally manage to capture the unit where the litter is falling from, NEA is often unable to take enforcement actions because it is not able to identify the offender.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With the new presumption clause, which presumes that the registered owner or the tenant of the flat is the offender, it will greatly increase the enforcement efficiency.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: More importantly, this presumption clause can serve as a deterrent, allowing family members and tenants living under the same roof to monitor one another.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The presumption will not affect 99% of the law-abiding HDB residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In fact, it will be helpful in reducing the inconvenience brought by high-rise littering.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In the market, we know that there are many affordable and effective cameras.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With this new rule in place, can NEA consider doubling the number of cameras to better monitor high-rise littering?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: NEA also said earlier that elderly offenders and children will be treated more leniently when enforcing the law.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But, in my constituency of Nanyang, there are cases of repeated high-rise littering offences committed by children.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State, how many high-rise littering offenders were committed by the elderly and underaged residents in the past five years?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We know that high-rise littering does not occur only in HDB estates, but also in private condominiums, with some even involving fatal casualties.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, let me move on to the other topic of Progressive Wage Model (PWM) which also constitute an important part of the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is an important question as Singaporeans have already experienced high inflation in the past year and the inflation rate is likely to remain high in the next one year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, I would also like to ask the Senior Minister of State, are there plans to justify the increase in wages by increasing the productivity of the sector with better-trained workers and technology?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Notwithstanding the above queries, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: High-rise littering has been on the rise with no signs of abating.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our cleaners bear the brunt of such inconsiderate and wanton behavior.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are often blamed for not maintaining the neighborhood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But ultimately, cleaners do not dirty the estate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: High-rise litterbugs cause real dangers to innocent passers-by too.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I agree wholeheartedly with the hon Mr Liang that the number of complaints is probably on the more conservative side.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Help the cleaners, take the fight to the litterbugs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are too many dwelling units for effective comprehensive enforcement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Owners and tenants must be made responsible for the action of their dwellers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To rebut the statutory presumption, the presumed offender must respond within 14 days of being notified by NEA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry clarify if this letter will only be sent via post?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If so, can NEA tap on the Government's digital capabilities to have the letter of intended prosecution to be sent electronically via email and SMS based on the registered owner or tenant's contact details in their Singpass?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would reduce vexatious cases and appeals where presumed offenders request for a longer timeline to rebut the statutory presumption by claiming that they had not seen the letter from NEA due to various reasons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Corrective Work Orders (CWOs) may also be discretionally imposed by Courts where they are satisfied that it is expedient to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Under what circumstances would it be considered expedient?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I join the hon Mr Lim Biow Chuan in urging the Ministry to consider imposing mandatory CWOs, alongside the current fine structure for high-rise littering.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, where the high-rise litterbug disposes of an item which has the propensity to cause grave bodily harm, perhaps the Courts should also have the discretion to impose a jail term.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that this distinction is important to hold high-rise litterbugs to a higher responsibility for their actions compared to general littering in public places.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, on surveillance camera deployments to aid NEA's efforts in taking enforcement action against high-rise litterbugs, could the Ministry share the challenges in deploying cameras for surveillance?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry also accept user-submitted video recordings as evidence for enforcement?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the proper safeguards in place, can NEA consider working with the Singapore Police Force to tap on its network of cameras?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This widens the surveillance capabilities without adding to the cost of deployment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, a framework can be put in place to balance the needs adroitly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on the revised cleaning business licensing framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The tiered licensing framework is a clear signal that we want companies to ready themselves with the right resources and practices to develop the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Critical to the success of this framework must be the rewards or premium in having a higher class licence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There must be economic rewards for companies that obtain the Class 1 license.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, only holders of a higher class licence can bid for certain projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This creates the financial incentives for companies to upgrade themselves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There might not be such a market for these higher class licences now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we can start to create one by having the public sector to commit to buying services from higher class license holders for projects of a set monetary threshold.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Larger firms with progressive practices can also adopt such practices, especially those which supply services to the public sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The challenges for businesses to transform and transition are also not trivial.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To support the changes to the revised framework, businesses should capitalise on the initiatives under the Environmental Services Industry Transformation Map and Jobs Transformation Map.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, businesses could ride on the push towards Outcome Based Contracting (OBCs), where service buyers specify contract requirements in terms of deliverable outcomes instead of headcount.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The tripartite partners can encourage the take-up of the Environmental Services Job Redesign Consultancy Package.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Substantial funding support is provided through the Productivity Solutions Grant to help businesses transform by streamlining operations alongside the adoption of technological solutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Cleaning and Waste Management industries face an urgent need to transform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are difficult industries that are shunned by most locals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Without the better use of technology, a rapidly ageing Singapore will face even more dire manpower challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a critical success in the ongoing work to improve the lives and livelihoods of locals working in this difficult but very essential industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our workers in the cleaning and waste management industries are clearly an indispensable part of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are more than deserving of better wages and brighter prospects in the long term.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The tripartite partners have shown their commitment to ensure this with various programmes and initiatives available to these businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will need to keep the momentum going to help our workers with better jobs and better pay to face the evolving challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The fall in number of tickets issued would highly be due to the curtailment of social activities during COVID-19 as the number of tickets issued are only for those who have been caught littering.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The real problem of littering is likely to remain and it would be interesting to see what this number would be in 2022 and 2023 as more of society opens up.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As one of the most densely populated countries in the world, with the majority of our population living in high-rise apartments or flats, the issue of high-rise littering is also of concern.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is interesting – compared to the fall in the number of tickets issued by NEA for littering in public spaces for 2020 and 2021, the same period saw a drastic increase in numbers of complaints for high-rise littering.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is likely because of more people working from home, thereby exacerbating the issue of litter being thrown out of the windows of their apartments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is almost as if they shifted their mindset from littering in public to littering from their apartments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The problem of high-rise littering needs to be addressed urgently because the actions of a few inconsiderate individuals can lead to the reduction in the quality of life for the rest of the residents in that entire block of flats.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In more severe cases, high-rise killer litter might lead to a loss of life when pedestrians are struck by them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, the burden of proof for high-rise littering lies in NEA having to identify and prove that an individual has committed the offence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The evidence is obtained from surveillance cameras that NEA deploys and flat owners only have to furnish NEA with the identity of every occupier of the flat at the time of the offence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The onus is on NEA to establish the identity of the culprits and taking punitive actions against the offenders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Clearly, this is an onerous process that is not only resource intensive but is inefficient as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That said, Mr Speaker, the prerequisite for enforcement actions remain – there is a need for NEA to deploy surveillance cameras to collect evidence that high-rise litter originated from a particular household.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With surveillance cameras being a scarce resource, I understand from Senior Minister of State Amy Khor's speech earlier that members of the public are allowed to submit footage of high-rise littering that the NEA could use to follow up on such cases.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The question I have for the Senior Minister of State and for the Government regarding this is, first of all, is there a convenient platform or a convenient app, a convenient website where the public can submit this evidence fairly easily and is fuss-free, and is it made known to the public?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think if the latter is the case, then it might actually deter some individuals from providing evidence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, in this regard, would the Government consider the evidence submitted to be sufficient without having to require the person submitting the evidence to go to Court to provide testimony?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I would like to move on to the extent of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, the Environmental and Public Health Bill applies only to publicly accessible areas.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Private properties such as executive condominiums and private strata condominiums are regarded as places with restricted access, hence, they are not subjected to the Bill unless the high-rise litter lands on public property.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was further suggested that cases of high-rise littering in such properties should be dealt with by the management committee with the properties’ by-law or the management committee can turn to the Courts to deal with recalcitrant individuals who persist in high-rise littering.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe the hon Member Mr Ang Wei Neng had also alluded to this in his speech.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2019, a television was thrown out of a 10th floor condominium unit.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2020, a television, sound bar and speakers were thrown out of a 50th floor condominium unit.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Maybe he was unhappy with his sound system – I do not know.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But as incredible, as it sounds, these things do happen.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While these incidents may seem isolated and extreme instances of high-rise littering, they demonstrate that high-rise littering and potentially killer litter can also be a problem in private properties as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government consider providing residents and management committees of private properties a more direct route to resolve such cases instead of them having to rely on the route of by-laws and taking the matter to Court, or Court orders?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, I understand that CWOs are not mandatory and they are only one possible form of punishment for those found guilty of littering.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These essential workers are often unseen and unheard and the PWM will help create a roadmap for upward progression.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a few clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Licensing sets entry-level baseline standards for cleaning businesses as the industry plays an important role in ensuring a clean and hygienic environment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three classes of licences are being introduced, replacing the current framework which only has one type of licence, renewable on an annual basis.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This tiered framework means that cleaning companies have to be committed to the industry and their employees, otherwise the licence will not be renewed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Between office and commercial, food and beverage (F&B), or the conservancy sub-sectors, which does NEA foresee being most affected in terms of the provision of services and also potential loss of jobs?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And does NEA have any plans to help cleaning companies and their employees make this transition?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Further, I understand that this paid-up capital requirement is being introduced to support better wages and greater technological adoption in the industry, but given that technological development and adoption requires more than just capital – for example, R&D and expertise which smaller companies may not have existing capacity for – does NEA have any schemes in mind to help these companies embrace technology?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a similar vein, it is of utmost importance to make upskilling resources accessible to all resident workers, especially for those who may be older and not as tech-savvy or may not be fluent in English.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How many WSQ courses are available in a non-English language and are these courses easily accessible and packaged as bite-sized to workers who need them?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such provisions would go a long way in helping workers upskill and grow regardless of background.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, on to our day-to-day living environments and the enforcement of high-rise littering.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: According to NEA, there has been a significant increase in such reports islandwide.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That said, practical problems may arise when trying to enforce this new law.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, home owners may be overseas or otherwise uncontactable in the 14-day window by which they have to show that they are not responsible for littering.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may not be able to satisfactorily prove their innocence if they are out of the house but leave no digital or paper footprint.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What steps will NEA take to reasonably clear home owners of this suspicion?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, some cases of high-rise littering cannot be stopped by enforcement alone if they are caused by other underlying issues.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, repeat offenders may have mental health conditions or disabilities and some seniors have very deep-seated beliefs that are challenging for family members to correct.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, a case of a resident who has dementia and throws items out of the window despite the best reminders from officers and family members, or seniors who continue to feed pigeons because they think it results in good karma.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In such cases, I urge NEA to understand the difficult position of home owners and exercise compassion in the enforcement process.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Enforcement should be solutions-driven to also soothe the frayed nerves of the complaining neighbour, such as installing mesh over the window for example, rather than focusing on a penal effect in such cases.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there a tiered process which NEA could employ, for example, a warning letter and advisory notice before the actual enforcement in Court?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, I understand that the high-rise littering act is proven to be committed from a residential flat when there is photo or video evidence that the littering has originated from that unit.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand from Senior Minister of State Amy Khor's speech earlier that genuine photos and videos supplied by neighbours and members of the public could be considered for evidence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But what is the standard of evidence required so that the public can help and chip in as eyes and ears on the ground, and who can the public submit these photos to?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Enforcement relies heavily on the deployment of cameras, which may be expensive, and already lean manpower.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I wonder if NEA plans to direct more resources to tackle this and if other individuals can be trained to support the enforcement too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three years can be a long time for investigations to be ongoing, both from the perspective of Government resources and also for the companies to have this outstanding.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employers, workers and everyday citizens alike must continue to play our part towards a clean Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the new law, I am hopeful that households or co-tenants would be more motivated to prevent littering.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate that NEA will exercise care when investigating cases committed by young children, the elderly and vulnerable groups who may claim to have mental conditions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am concerned that if NEA just issues warnings to cases with mental conditions, the fundamental problem of littering and its associated safety risks remains.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support that these offenders be required to attend assessments within a stipulated timeframe.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If no valid reason is provided to explain their absence, they should be deemed guilty of having committed high-rise littering.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have a case in my constituency where a gentleman does high-rise littering on a daily basis for the past few years.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The tissue papers and plastic bags are stuck on trees and may pose health hazards to the residents staying on the second and third levels.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When NEA, Town Councils, workers, community volunteers and myself approached the family members on various occasions, they often claim that the house owner is mentally unsound and they cannot control his behaviour.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We enlisted the help of a Government agency in the hope that it can perform the assessment and refer this culprit to IMH.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Government agency involves the Family Service Centre (FSC) which spoke to his wife as the uncle is always hiding inside the room or the toilet.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The wife also has concerns about the treatment partly because of the medications' side effects he had experienced previously.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This FSC informed that such littering behaviour does not warrant a need for enforced treatment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, high-rise littering is not a sufficient reason to get the Police to compel the owner to open the door.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Meanwhile, the neighbours continue to experience such disamenities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I would like to know how this amendment will abate such littering cases.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I suspect that in some cases, the offenders may not necessarily have any mental conditions, just the bad personal habit of littering.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to seek a clarification.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to ask the Ministry if such fines have been effective against recalcitrant offenders?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What happens when they plead financial hardship as the reason for being unable to pay and yet continue littering?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): The Bill makes it an offence to cause or permit the dumping or disposal of waste in a public place from 1 July onwards.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have had cases in my estate where the contractors and residents threw bulky items into the pneumatic waste conveyance systems and caused blockages for the entire precinct for days.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, the paid-up capital requirement was introduced to ensure that operators can keep up with wage climbs under the cleaning sector's existing Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for the long haul and adopt more technological solutions which can be costly.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that the Government agencies which engage cleaning services from Class 1 licensees do not pass on the costs to Singaporeans indirectly as many are struggling with inflation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also appeal to the Ministry to provide grants so as to assist these deserving companies in their purchases of expensive equipments to improve productivity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The thoughtful, and I would like to add, passionate comments and suggestions reflect the high regard we place on public health and in maintaining high standards of public cleanliness and sanitation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, on the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for the waste management sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To achieve this, we also require companies to invest in training and technology adoption.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A more competent waste management workforce will benefit our waste management companies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This upgrading of the waste management industry will, ultimately, benefit all Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We acknowledge that there will be some increase in operational cost initially, as Mr Ang Wei Neng has spoken about.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To moderate the increase, the Government has provided the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) which waste management companies can tap on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In the medium to longer term, investment in our workers will pay off for our companies by enhancing their capabilities, productivity and efficiency.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even as the Government provides some transitional support, we will need to do our part as service buyers and consumers to bear some of the cost increase in order to support our lower-wage waste management workers on their upskilling journey.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Tripartite Cluster for Waste Management had made a conscious effort to offer better wages to attract new entrants and retain the existing experienced workforce, and to couple this with higher skills requirements to drive greater productivity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: On Mr Yip Hon Weng's questions, it is not a common practice for waste management companies to deploy outsourced workers from manpower supplying companies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The proposed amendments to prevent such a practice will ensure that all waste management workers benefit from the PWM wages.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As for extending the PWM to other sub-sectors, we do have plans to cover the waste treatment and disposal sub-sector at a later stage.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I agree with Ms Joan Pereira that partnerships are key in achieving our zero-waste vision.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Individuals and organisations may tap on initiatives such as the SG Eco Fund for projects that support environmental sustainability and involve the community, and NEA's 3R Fund for projects that reduce waste generation and disposal.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As for Ms Poh Li San's suggestion to move towards a user-pays principle for waste collection, a similar model has already been adopted for trade premises where the monthly fee is based on the waste output by volume.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to study different models for waste collection fees but there are currently no plans to adopt such a model for households.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Instead, we encourage households to reduce waste and recycle more through education and other policies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members have also raised clarifications and suggestions on PWM that apply to both the waste management and cleaning sectors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: On waste management, Mr Don Wee asked how we will ensure that resident workers will receive the PWM wage increments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The PWM requirements are implemented through the licensing regime for waste management licensees.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Applicants for a waste management licence must show a progressive wage plan that they will be or are paying their workers PWM wages and produce relevant documents as required.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will conduct regular checks and impose financial penalties in the event of non-compliance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In serious cases, the licence may be suspended or revoked.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A similar approach has been taken for the cleaning sector's PWM, which is also implemented through the licensing regime for cleaning businesses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked about making skills upgrading more accessible to workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Employers can tap on the Workfare Skills Support Scheme, which provides funding support such as absentee payroll to employers who send eligible workers for approved courses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For the cleaning sector, NEA works with the NTUC U-Care Centre to encourage service buyers to support their service providers who wish to send their cleaners for training during working hours and call on service buyers to refrain from requesting for replacement headcounts if cleaning standards are not compromised.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether the PWM would be extended to migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The purpose of implementing the PWM requirements for resident workers in the waste management sector, as stated in the proposed amendments, is to ensure a more engaged waste collection and waste disposal workforce and the retention of a core of resident waste management workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In developing the broader PWM for other sectors and not just those in environmental services, it is recognised that employers are already responsible for the additional costs of the migrant workers, including their healthcare, accommodation and other related costs during their stay in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As such, employers are not required to adhere to the PWM for their migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nonetheless, employers are encouraged to adopt the principles of the PWM for their migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members have spoken extensively about the revised cleaning business licensing framework.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the goals and benefits of the revised framework and our plans to achieve them, while Mr Don Wee, Ms Nadia Samdin and Ms Ng Ling Ling raised concerns about increased business costs and possible folding of businesses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The revised framework is a strategic initiative under the Environmental Services Industry Transformation Map (ES ITM) to build more capable businesses in environmental services and spur them to create quality jobs and careers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With the Class 3 licence retaining the same requirements as the current licensing scheme, the revised cleaning business licensing framework will not impose higher barriers to entry compared to today.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These changes are key to raising the capabilities of the cleaning industry, which will benefit both the businesses as well as service buyers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Given their ability to meet the higher minimum paid-up capital requirement and the additional training requirements relating to Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ), Class 1 licensees provide greater assurance to service buyers that they are equipped with more resources, experience and capabilities to undertake larger cleaning contracts and are committed to uplifting the wages and competencies of our cleaners.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To cope with the mandatory PWM wage increases for low-wage cleaners, cleaning businesses may tap on the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme for transitional wage support.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We expect all cleaning businesses hiring resident workers to benefit from this scheme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This gives existing cleaning business licensees more time, in fact, effectively up to three years from today until 2026, to eventually transit to a Class 2 or 1 licence.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nevertheless, we recognise that there may be some degree of industry consolidation that favours companies with stronger capabilities and are better able to meet their employment obligations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In this transition, NEA will ensure that there are sufficient safeguards to protect cleaners who may be displaced.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition to giving existing cleaning businesses sufficient runway to transit, NEA will work closely with Workforce Singapore and NTUC U-Care Centre to facilitate job transfers within the Environmental Services industry, if needed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To Mr Louis Ng's question on compliance history, the proposed requirement is that in order to attain a Class 1 licence, cleaning businesses must not have any non-compliance with relevant written laws in the last 24 months.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Only Court conviction history, including those related to payment of wages to employees, will be taken into account.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Overall, the new requirements have been calibrated to provide service buyers and workers with the assurance that the businesses have the financial stability as well as capabilities and practices to deliver reliable and quality cleaning services without being overly onerous on business owners.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will continue to review the licensing framework as necessary and will take Mr Louis Ng's suggestions into consideration.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Several Members, including Ms Joan Pereira, asked about the support for cleaning businesses to adopt technology and raise productivity, including working with Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to build competencies in the cleaning industry.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Beyond the ES ITM, there are various Government initiatives supporting innovation and technology adoption.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Chief Technology Officer-as-a-Service is a platform that helps cleaning businesses boost digitalisation efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Cleaning businesses can also benefit from the National Robotics Programme to develop new cleaning technology.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, the Autonomous Environmental Services Vehicle, which facilitates cleaning through robotic road-sweeping, was developed this way.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To build competencies, NEA has been working with IHLs to equip cleaners with digital skills such as using robotics systems to improve operations and processes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To better address learning needs, Ms Nadia Samdin would be pleased to know that some training courses are offered in languages such as Mandarin and Malay, while some training providers deploy multilingual trainers for their courses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will continue to partner IHLs and SkillsFuture Singapore to enhance training offerings for the cleaning workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some have asked how this would be applied.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the effectiveness of the new law and other plans to address high-rise littering.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As highlighted in my opening speech, the statutory presumptions will place greater onus on owners and tenants of residential flats to prevent littering acts from being committed from their units in the first place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We believe this will enhance deterrence and contribute to reducing the number of high-rise littering acts in the long run.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Darryl David and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the scope of the statutory presumptions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For high-rise littering committed from the common corridors and staircases of residential flats, NEA will continue to investigate such cases based on the current approach.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The statutory presumptions also apply if litter is thrown from a private apartment that is used for residential purpose and the litter lands in a public place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For high-rise littering within condominium or private apartment estates, Management Corporation Strata Titles (MCSTs) can introduce and leverage their by-laws to take appropriate actions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked about the method of issuance of the letter of intended prosecution to owners or tenants.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At the earlier stage of investigation, NEA will send a letter via post to notify the owner or tenant of the offence and explain how the statutory presumption will apply during the legal proceedings for the offence and how it may be rebutted.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Contact via email or phone would only be possible after email addresses or phone numbers are furnished by the owners or tenants when they respond to the initial letter and request for subsequent correspondence via such methods.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Wan Rizal also asked whether owners or tenants could have more time – 30 days instead of 14 days – to rebut the presumption.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The time period of 14 days is necessary to ensure that owners or tenants provide timely information to NEA to investigate the case effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, NEA will consider the facts of each appeal for more time to respond on a case-by-case basis when deciding whether or not to proceed with the enforcement action.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In response to Mr Leon Perera's query on the burden of proof for rebutting the presumption, there is no requirement for proving beyond reasonable doubt.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, to prove that the owner or tenant was not at home, evidence such as purchase receipts or transportation trip transactions can be produced.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Alternatively, in response to Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin's question, the owner or tenant can provide the identity of the person whom he or she reasonably believes to be the offender to rebut the presumption.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In response to Mr Leon Perera, merely pointing the finger at another person without a reasonable basis will not be acceptable.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Concerns were raised on how the statutory presumption may negatively affect the dynamics of interpersonal relationships and fairness in investigations, such as possible instances where owners or tenants pin the responsibility on children or on the elderly and disabled individuals to avoid the penalties.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In cases involving multiple owners or tenants, given that NEA will send the letter of intended prosecution to all registered owners and tenants individually, each owner or tenant can respond directly to NEA.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Individuals found to knowingly provide false information to implicate another person can be charged for providing false information.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will be judicious and exercise care in investigating and resolving cases involving vulnerable groups such as young children and the elderly, as is already practised today.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For littering acts committed by children below the age of 12, NEA will not take enforcement action against them as they may not have sufficient maturity to understand what they had done.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently, NEA will issue an advisory letter to the parents to underscore their responsibility to educate their child on binning litter properly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As for offenders with mental incapacity, NEA refers such cases to social welfare agencies, such as the Agency for Integrated Care, to provide more holistic help with the consent of the offender, or if the offender is not capable of giving such consent, then his or her next-of-kin.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The social welfare agencies may then work with relevant stakeholders such as IMH for medical assessments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For persistent cases involving the vulnerable groups, NEA may engage the parents or households to implement measures to prevent high-rise littering such as installing wire mesh on their windows.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While we empathise with the families of offenders with mental incapacity, NEA may still proceed with prosecution of persistent cases with the Attorney-General's Chambers' concurrence, especially if the offender is aware of the nature and consequences of his or her actions and no effort is made to prevent recurrence.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some Members asked about the effectiveness of NEA's surveillance cameras.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA does not track the data for individuals with mental or physical disabilities, which only forms a minority of offenders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The catch-rate is constrained by factors such as the suitability of the vantage points for camera deployment, lighting conditions and quality of information received through feedback.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Liang Eng Hwa may be pleased to know that NEA's surveillance cameras already leverage video analytics to detect falling litter, allowing for flagging and notification of high-rise littering acts without the need to manually review hours of video footages.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will continue to enhance its enforcement capabilities by keeping pace with developments in surveillance camera technology.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If the Court is satisfied that it would be appropriate for the protection of the environment and rehabilitation of the offender, the offender may also be issued with a Corrective Work Order (CWO).

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To Members' suggestion to make the CWO mandatory for all littering offenders, the current fines remain an effective deterrent.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will continue to monitor the situation and review the penalty regime where necessary.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To Mr Don Wee's query, for recalcitrant offenders who appeal to NEA due to financial hardship, NEA will assess the facts of the case and the offender's past offences before taking the appropriate actions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This may include offering a composition sum or not acceding to the appeal.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To deter such offenders from littering again, NEA ensures that the enforcement actions are commensurate with the severity of the offence.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked if a new clause could be included to provide a jail term in addition to fines if the items littered have the propensity to cause harm.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: HDB exercises the right of compulsory acquisition sparingly and as a last resort.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nevertheless, this measure may also not address the root of the issue if the offender is just forced to move out and commits high-rise littering at a new address.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There are suggestions for NEA to accept evidence of littering from residential flats submitted by members of the public.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As I shared earlier, clear evidence that an act of littering had been committed from an identified flat must be provided.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members of the public can provide such evidence through channels such as myENV or the OneService mobile applications.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will follow up and investigate the littering offence as long as the quality of the evidence is able to support NEA's enforcement action.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked if residents are allowed to install cameras pointing upwards and not directly into their neighbours' units to identify high-rise littering offenders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: While residents may undertake measures to support NEA, we encourage residents to be mindful of community relations and respect the privacy of their neighbours, as installing cameras within one's unit may intrude into his or her neighbours' privacy or interfere with his or her neighbours' enjoyment or use of their homes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Residents should seek Town Councils' approval prior to installing any camera in HDB common spaces given that this is regulated under Town Council by-laws.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Lastly, Mr Louis Ng asked if a similar statutory presumption could be used to address the problem of second-hand smoke in flats.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As explained earlier, the statutory presumption proposed in this Bill first requires clear evidence that an act of littering has been committed from a specific residential flat.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Unlike high-rise littering acts which involve undisputed evidence of littering from a flat, obtaining proof of the acts of smoking at windows and balconies is technologically inordinately more challenging.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition to finding suitable locations for the deployment of surveillance cameras to detect smoking at windows and balconies, such cameras would need to detect the heat signature of a smoker's lit cigarette and visually identify that the lit object is a cigarette.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The cameras that need to be used have a much shorter range and their line of sight can be easily blocked when smokers stand further from the windows or stand behind a glass pane, curtains or any physical barriers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides the limitations of current heat detection camera technology, this proposal gives rise to privacy issues as the entire footage recorded may have to be reviewed manually, even if it is by authorised persons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These challenges need to be overcomed before we can consider prohibiting smoking at windows and balconies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I have explained this at length in this House on many occasions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But in order to not disappoint the Member, I am explaining this again.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And since then, we have yet to see practicable solutions, from our scanning of available technology as well as international developments, to address second-hand smoke coming from homes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nonetheless, I would like to assure Mr Louis Ng that we will continue to monitor developments in this area with regard to smoking in homes because we are also as concerned about second-hand smoke and the harm it causes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I shall move on to the rest of the amendments in this Bill.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Town Councils can introduce a by-law to make causing blockages of PWCS an offence and develop ways of enforcing against this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The PWCS chute hopper is designed such that bulky items, for example large or long items, would not be able to fit into the opening.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Sensors and monitoring equipment also help to prevent an excessive piling up of refuse within the chute.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Residents and contractors are reminded that bulky waste can be conveniently disposed of by contacting their respective Town Councils for assistance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh sought clarification on the cost of installing PWCS and how it compares with the potential savings in labour cost.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the disposal of waste in the common areas of HDB blocks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Disposing of waste in HDB common areas, except in areas designated for refuse, contravenes the respective Town Council's by-laws.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Residents wishing to dispose of bulky items may also contact their respective Town Councils for assistance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Complex cases include those involving multiple interviewees, some of whom may be uncooperative, thereby prolonging investigations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Notwithstanding the amendment, NEA will ensure that our investigation processes remain efficient.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have come a long way since Independence, working hard to keep Singapore clean.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This was made possible by the tireless efforts of generations of Singaporeans, including our cleaners and waste management workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Not only has this benefited our health and well-being, being a clean and green city has become part of our national identity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We must cherish what we have and continue to be guided by the values of care and consideration to keep our environment clean.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The proposed changes, as set out in this Bill, will enable us to support our cleaning and waste management sectors, as well as strengthen our shared responsibility to cultivate right behaviours that safeguard public health and a clean environment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, I call on all Members of this House to support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Also, thank you to Senior Minister of State Dr Amy Khor for the very comprehensive round-up.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I am heartened that NEA is using artificial intelligence (AI) to analyse the video images and not human beings.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And I also note that NEA deployed 200 cameras onsite.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: And I understand that each camera typically covered about 14 days of operation, which means NEA probably has more than 100 sets of cameras.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I have alluded in my speech on whether NEA can consider doubling or tripling the number of cameras it has, so as to make sure that every repeated complaint about the locations of high-rise littering, would have a chance of detecting the culprits.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: But will Senior Minister of State Dr Amy Khor share how many are repeat offenders and how do we deal with them, even though they are elderly or young?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As I have shared, installing surveillance cameras depends on the design of the block, which stack the suspect is in, whether it is possible to find a suitable location.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, sometimes, it is not a question of the number of cameras available but whether we have got good quality information and whether we are able to deploy and install the camera in a location that gives us a good chance of a successful catch.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And that is because there are all these constraints, whether it is weather, design of the block, quality of information and so on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As far as we are concerned, if there is good reason to install a surveillance camera, we will do so.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, it is not a question of increasing the numbers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But as I have also said, putting surveillance camera everywhere and all the time is really not sustainable; it is not something we can do.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Enforcing against high-rise littering, as we have also said, is very laborious; it is resource-intensive and also requires lots of time.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We need to see how we can do this effectively.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But, actually, the best way to address this problem is by cultivating positive social norms, civic-mindedness and social responsibility.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am not quite sure what he was asking – repeat offenders and so on?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Yes, I am talking about the repeat offenders, those who are below 19 and those who are elderly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I just wanted to ask the Senior Minister of State, with the cases of littering are going up, why does the Senior Minister of State think that imposing fines will act as an effective deterrent against littering?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: We are not asking them to go to jail.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: We are asking them to experience what it is like to have to pick up litter and watch for themselves the effect of littering on the common areas.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: So, why is NEA so against issuing CWOs, even for the first offence?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Member had submitted a similar Parliamentary Question and we had also said that because the number of repeat offenders is so low, we do want to give the first-time offenders a second chance.      .
